name: Dot Ruskin

inspiration.oldScript: The Slumber Party Massacre sent an escaped killer with a giant power drill after teenage girls in nightgowns at a sleepover, the drill standing in for the camera's leer and the girls punished for having a party at all. It was written as a feminist parody of exactly that, then shot and sold as the very exploitation it was mocking.
inspiration.newLens: Here the danger lands on the fraternity boys who made sleepover girls a punchline. Rehearsing a sincere drag night, in heels and wigs, they learn the damsel's fear from the inside: the snapped heel, the dead phone, the stairs that go up instead of out. The drag is never the joke, and the brothers who commit to it are the ones who make it to morning. The "monster" is the shop-class girl the town blamed for fighting back, and the crew wins by making the house give back what it took and say sorry.

logline: All Halloween week the brothers of Gamma Rho are rehearsing a drag night to fix the Glitter Box's leaky roof, and every night the power dies, the phone goes dead, the doors are drilled shut from outside, and a girl in coveralls and pink curlers walks the halls with her late father's electric drill, come back for what the house stole in 1966. The brother who calls it all a joke is the first to vanish.
backstory: Two miles past Crystal Street, at the dead end of Old Quarry Road, sags the Gamma Rho house: a peeling Victorian that Valley State College's oldest fraternity has rented since 1948. For eighteen Halloweens, starting in 1949, the brothers kept a tradition they called the Raid. Every October 31 they pulled on rubber monster masks, burst into a girls' slumber party, chased the girls out of their sleeping bags into the cold yard with flashlights in their faces, and drove off with "trophies": sleeping bags, locked diaries, spare flannel pajamas from their overnight bags, coffee cans of curlers. The haul went into a glass case in the front hall with a brass plate for every year. In 1966 the Raid hit the Halvorsen farmhouse across the road, where six Glimmer Falls High seniors were sleeping over. One of them was Dorothy "Dot" Ruskin, seventeen, the first girl ever to take shop at Glimmer Falls High, who wore her coveralls over her pajamas because she had come straight from the bench. That week she had won the Industrial Arts Fair blue ribbon for a cedar hope chest with hand-cut dovetails, and she had wheeled the chest over on her dad's hand truck to show the girls, the ribbon pinned to its lid. The boys took her blue ribbon off it too. While they were whooping in the yard, Dot found the trunk of their convertible stuffed with the girls' things, plugged her late father's electric drill into the Halvorsens' porch outlet and drilled out the trunk lock. She got back two sleeping bags before the car peeled away. She never touched a single boy. The college paper ran a photo of the grinning brothers under the headline HARMLESS FUN, and a dean said boys will be boys. The town paper said a local girl had come at college men with a power tool. Glimmer Falls High crossed her name off the judging sheet and expelled her for conduct unbecoming a young lady. The Raid ended that year, quietly, with no announcement, but the trophies never went back, and nobody ever said sorry. That winter Dot walked up Old Quarry Road one last time, knocked on the Gamma Rho door, and asked, politely, for the girls' things. Nobody answered. Two miles away the Heartstone hummed, and kept everything she felt on that porch. By morning there was only a coffee can of curlers on the step. Dot was Taken, stuck at seventeen inside the one night she never got to finish. Now it is 1986, and the brothers are doing something new: a sincere drag night fundraiser for the Glitter Box, coached by Glory Hallelujah herself. The Heartstone has woken and let Dot out, exactly as she was that night: coveralls over red plaid pajamas, pink foam curlers, safety goggles, and her father's chrome drill on a frayed cord that finds an outlet in every room and whines through the walls. She wants what the house took. And she wants to hear it say two words.

centralIssue.title: Boys will be boys
centralIssue.summary: Gamma Rho humiliated sleepover girls for eighteen Halloweens and called it tradition, and when one shop-class girl fought back with the only tool she had, the town called her the dangerous one, took away her ribbon and her place at the workbench, and called the boys harmless fun. The trophies are still in the glass case, and the house has never apologized. Dot is not angry that the brothers are in wigs; she is angry that nobody ever gave anything back. Read what the papers said, find the ribbon the school crossed out, hear Dot's side from someone who knew her, then make the house return every trophy, say sorry out loud, and give Dot the seat at the workbench she was denied.

poster: a lanky freckled translucent teenage girl in oil-stained blue coveralls over red plaid flannel pajamas, pink foam curlers in her short dark hair, round safety goggles glowing amber, standing at the top of a creaking Victorian staircase holding a chrome 1950s electric hand drill raised toward the ceiling, its long frayed cord trailing off into the dark, sawdust drifting in a flashlight beam, below her on the stairs a gangly young man in a towering blond wig, bold fire-engine-red lipstick and a sequined gown holding up one snapped high heel like a weapon, other young men in wigs and sparkly dresses crowding behind him, a glowing glass trophy case of sleeping bags, diaries and curlers in the hallway, a full moon through a window crossed with screwed-on plywood
portrait: Close portrait of a lanky freckled translucent teenage girl in oil-stained blue coveralls over red plaid flannel pajamas, pink foam curlers in her short dark hair, pushing round amber safety goggles up onto her forehead to reveal tired, stubborn eyes, sawdust on her cheek, a red bandana knotted at her throat, the chrome nose of an old electric hand drill raised beside her face, lit by a flashlight beam from below and a magenta glow from a dusty hallway
endingPhoto: a lanky freckled translucent teenage girl in oil-stained blue coveralls over red plaid flannel pajamas, pink foam curlers in her short dark hair, round safety goggles glowing amber, posed on a Victorian staircase landing holding an old chrome electric drill high toward the ceiling, curlers flying, facing a defiant line of young men in sequined gowns and feather boas with arms linked on the stairs below her, the one in front in a towering blond wig holding one snapped red high-heeled shoe up high in triumph, a glowing glass trophy case and a doorway crossed with screwed-on boards behind them, a huge moon in the window
taunts: Measure twice, cut once. I've had twenty years to measure you boys.
Righty tighty, lefty loosey. Every door in this house is righty tighty now.
Boys will be boys, huh? Funny. Nobody ever said girls will be girls.
You kept my blue ribbon in a glass box. I kept my drill.
Two words. That's all. Give it back and say them, and I'll unplug.

clues.title: "Harmless fun"
clues.hint: The library keeps the Valley State College paper and the Glimmer Falls Gazette on microfilm. Look at the first week of November, 1966.

encounter.title: November 1966
encounter.place: The microfilm room, Glimmer Falls Public Library
encounter.text: The microfilm reader hums in a windowless room at the back of the library. The reel labeled VALLEY STATE CLARION, FALL 1966 is warm to the touch, and a fine curl of sawdust sits in the bottom of its box, though nothing in this room is wood. Ms. Hart watches from the doorway with her arms folded. "Gamma Rho," she says, before you have even threaded it. "I wondered when somebody would ask."
encounter.art: A small windowless library microfilm room lit by the green glow of a humming reader, an open cardboard reel box on the table with a fine curl of pale sawdust inside, a teenager threading the warm reel, and a freckled 38-year-old librarian with gray-streaked chestnut hair, tortoiseshell glasses on a beaded chain and an oxblood cardigan leaning in the doorway with her arms folded, green screen light and dark walls, medium shot

choices.label: Thread the 1966 reel and roll to the first week of November

success.text: November 2, 1966, front page: a photo of grinning boys in rubber monster masks holding up pink sleeping bags and a diary like a fish they caught. HARMLESS FUN: GAMMA RHO'S HALLOWEEN RAID A HOWLING SUCCESS. "Boys will be boys," says the dean. You switch to the Gazette, two days later, page nine: LOCAL GIRL EXPELLED AFTER POWER TOOL INCIDENT. The witness quoted is Harold Thurston, 20. Dorothy Ruskin is not quoted at all. Nobody asked her.
success.art: A teenager at a glowing microfilm reader scrolling past an old newspaper photo of grinning young men in rubber monster masks holding up sleeping bags, a tiny second clipping visible on the next page

failure.text: The reel spins on its own, faster and faster, and every frame is the same photo: the grinning boys in their rubber masks, again and again, laughing at you. The bulb pops. In the dark the reader keeps whirring, and under the whir, faintly, a drill.
failure.art: A microfilm reader spinning wildly in a dark room, the same blurred photo of masked grinning young men flickering on the screen, a teenager backing away as the bulb bursts

choices.label: Ask Ms. Hart what she remembers about Dot Ruskin

success.text: Ms. Hart sits down heavily. "Dot fixed my bicycle chain behind the gym in the rain and would not take a dime. Then the Raid, and suddenly she was a menace. The boys got their picture in the paper. Dot got expelled. The Clarion called it harmless fun and the Gazette called her dangerous, and the only thing she ever did was want her things back." She pulls the reel for you herself, and her hands are shaking. "Girls who didn't fit this town learned that year what it would forgive, and who. I learned it twice."
success.art: A librarian in a cardigan sitting at a microfilm reader beside a teenager, threading a reel with unsteady hands, an old high school yearbook open on the desk between them

failure.text: "Not today," Ms. Hart says, too quickly, and turns off the reader. As you leave, every book cart in the stacks rattles at once, as if something is drilling up through the floor, and a single pink foam curler rolls out from under the card catalog and stops at your shoe.
failure.art: A pink foam hair curler rolling across library carpet to stop at a teenager's sneaker, book carts rattling in the stacks behind, a librarian turning away

clues.title: The crossed-out name
clues.hint: Glimmer Falls High's shop room still keeps the Industrial Arts Fair winners board and the old judging binders. The 1966 line is blank.

encounter.title: Shop Class, 1966
encounter.place: The shop room, Glimmer Falls High
encounter.text: The shop room smells of sawdust and machine oil, and the homecoming float sits half-built under a tarp. On the wall hangs the Industrial Arts Fair winners board, a brass plate for every year since 1960. The plate for 1966 has been pried off, leaving four empty screw holes. As you look at it, the drill press in the corner switches itself on, spins for exactly three seconds, and stops.
encounter.art: A high school shop room smelling of sawdust, wooden workbenches with iron vises, a pegboard of painted tool outlines, a half-built homecoming float under a blue tarp, a wall of small brass plates on a wooden board with one empty space showing four bare screw holes, a drill press in the corner spinning by itself, a teenager standing frozen by the board, dusty afternoon light through tall windows, wide shot

choices.label: Dig through the old judging binders in the tool crib

success.text: Behind the lumber rack, a box of binders. Industrial Arts Fair, October 1966. First Place: D. Ruskin, cedar hope chest, hand-cut dovetails. "Finest joinery I have judged in thirty years," the judge wrote. Then a red line through her name, and in a different hand: Disqualified. Conduct unbecoming a young lady. Ribbon not recovered. Stapled behind it, a carbon of her expulsion letter: The college assures us the young men involved meant no harm.
success.art: A teenager in a dusty tool crib reading an old judging sheet with a name struck through in red pen, a typed carbon letter stapled behind it, binders spilling from a box at their feet

failure.text: The bandsaw starts up behind you, then the lathe, then the drill press, every machine in the room whining at once while the pegboard rattles its tool outlines. You dive under a workbench until it stops. When you crawl out, every hammer on the board has been rehung, perfectly, in the right outline.
failure.art: Every machine in a dark school shop room running by itself, a bandsaw, lathe and drill press whining, a pegboard of tools rattling, a teenager crouched under a workbench

choices.label: Run your hand along the underside of the oldest workbench

success.text: Your fingers find carving in the wood, deep and careful: D.R. 1966. FIRST GIRL. NOT THE LAST. Beside it, wedged into the joint, a folded sheet: the original judging card, her name still unscratched, and the judge's note in the margin. "She did all the dovetails by hand. The boys used the router." Someone hid it there before the school could cross it out.
success.art: A teenager lying on their back under an old scarred workbench reading initials carved into the underside by flashlight, a folded paper wedged into the wooden joint

failure.text: A splinter the size of a toothpick drives into your palm, and the vise above you cranks itself shut with a groan. From the far end of the room comes a man's voice, crackly as an old intercom: "Miss Ruskin, home economics is down the hall." Then a girl's voice, right beside your ear: "I know where it is."
failure.art: A teenager wincing beneath a workbench clutching a splintered hand, a heavy iron vise cranking shut above them, an old intercom speaker on the shop wall

clues.title: The girl who fixed the lights
clues.hint: Glory Hallelujah has worked the Glitter Box since the sixties. Ask her who rewired the old follow spot in the booth.

encounter.title: The Follow Spot
encounter.place: The lighting booth, the Glitter Box Playhouse
encounter.text: Rain plinks into a dozen buckets across the Glitter Box stage, which is why Gamma Rho is raising money in the first place. Glory Hallelujah, in rehearsal sequins and fuzzy slippers, is on a ladder emptying one. High in the back of the house, the old follow spot clicks on by itself and swings slowly across the seats until its circle of light finds you. Glory looks up at it and goes very still. "Well," she says softly. "Hello, Dot."
encounter.art: An old vaudeville theater with rain dripping from the ceiling into a dozen metal buckets across the stage, a tall drag queen in rehearsal sequins and fuzzy slippers on a stepladder emptying one bucket, and from a high booth at the back of the house an old follow spot shining a hard circle of white light onto a teenager sitting alone in the empty red seats, dim gray house light and one white beam, wide shot

choices.label: Ask Glory who Dot was and what really happened

success.text: Glory climbs down and sits beside you. "Fall of sixty-six I was twenty-four and running these lights, and that spot was dead. A girl in coveralls rewired it in an afternoon for a plate of my mother's pierogi. The night after the Raid she came here shaking. Those boys had stuffed the girls' things in a car trunk, and Dot drilled out the lock to get them back. That's all she did, honey. She never laid a finger on a boy. She asked me why it was fun when they did it and dangerous when she did, and I didn't have an answer." Glory dabs one eye. "I've had a long time to think of one."
success.art: A tall drag queen in rehearsal sequins and fuzzy slippers sitting in a theatre seat beside a teenager, telling a story with one hand pressed to her heart, rain dripping into buckets on the stage below

failure.text: Glory opens her mouth, then shakes her head. "Not with that light on me, sugar." The spot snaps off. Every bucket on the stage overflows at once, and from the booth comes the long whine of a drill. Glory hustles you out the stage door. "Come back tomorrow. Bring cookies. Bring courage."
failure.art: Rain buckets overflowing across a dark theatre stage, a drag queen in sequins steering a teenager toward a glowing stage door, a high booth window glowing amber behind them

choices.label: Climb the catwalk ladder to the follow-spot booth

success.text: The booth is warm, the spot still ticking as it cools. Riveted to its side is a little brass plate: REWIRED BY D. RUSKIN, OCT 1966. Tucked behind the lamp housing is a folded page in neat block capitals: THINGS THEY TOOK. MARJORIE'S DIARY. LINDA'S SLEEPING BAG. PAT'S CURLERS. MY RIBBON. GOT 2 SLEEPING BAGS BACK OUT OF THE TRUNK. DRILLED THE LOCK. DIDN'T TOUCH ANYBODY. NOBODY ASKED ME.
success.art: A teenager in a cramped theatre lighting booth reading a folded handwritten list beside a warm old follow spot with a small brass plate riveted to its side, the dark empty theatre seats far below

failure.text: Halfway up, the ladder starts to shake, every bolt turning in its socket with a soft whir, righty tighty, lefty loosey. You slide down the last ten feet and land in a bucket of rainwater. Up in the booth, the spot swings away from you, as if disappointed.
failure.art: A teenager sliding down a rattling catwalk ladder in a dark theatre and landing with a splash in a rain bucket, a follow spot in a high booth swinging away

signature.title: Dress Rehearsal
signature.place: The Gamma Rho parlor, Old Quarry Road, 10 p.m.
signature.text: The parlor furniture has been shoved against the walls, and a runway of duct-taped card tables runs down the middle of the Gamma Rho house. Glory Hallelujah sits at the end like a judge, sequined arms folded. "Shoulders back, chin up, walk like the rent is due!" Reggie Okafor, the house president, follows his clipboard down the runway in a borrowed gold gown. Teddy Alvarado, the youngest pledge, already walks in heels better than anyone in the room. Moose is hemming a dress on the sewing machine by the fireplace. And Chad Pettigrew, a sweet, six-foot-three, terrified sophomore in a towering blond wig and Fire Engine Fantasy lipstick, wobbles on platform pumps two sizes too small. "I can do this," he whispers. "I am Lady Chadelier." Then every light in the house dims at once, the record player groans down to a crawl, and from somewhere inside the walls comes a thin, rising whine, like a dentist's drill the size of a house. A flashlight beam slides under the front door and sweeps slowly across the floor, looking for someone.
signature.art: A Victorian fraternity parlor at ten at night with the furniture shoved to the walls and a runway of duct-taped folding tables down the middle, young men in wigs and borrowed gowns frozen mid-walk, a tall drag queen in sequins judging from an armchair, a huge lineman with a curly mullet at a sewing machine by the fireplace, a gangly six-foot-three young man in a towering blond wig, red lipstick and too-small platform pumps wobbling, the lamps dimming and a flashlight beam sliding in under the front door, wide shot

choices.label: Spin the record by hand and keep the walk going: the show goes on

success.text: You spin the record with one finger, Glory snaps "WALK!", and the brothers walk, in the dark, one after another, Chad wobbling but never stopping, chin up. The whine in the walls falters. It slows, and stops, like whoever is inside the plaster has put down her tool to watch. The flashlight beam lingers on Chad's sequined hem for a long moment, then clicks off.
success.art: Young men in wigs and gowns strutting down a card-table runway in a dark parlor while a teenager spins a record by hand, a drag queen snapping her fingers, a flashlight beam resting on a sequined hem

failure.text: The record skips, the whine climbs, and the flashlight beam finds Chad. He shrieks and bolts, not out the front door but up the stairs, which every person who has ever seen a horror movie knows is wrong. You find him wedged into the second-floor linen closet, sequins glittering through the slats, and it takes three brothers and a plate of cookies to coax him out.
failure.art: Sequins glittering through the slats of a linen closet door on a dark Victorian landing, a flashlight beam sweeping the hall, brothers in wigs creeping up the stairs with a plate of cookies

choices.label: Press your ear to the wallpaper and follow the whine

success.text: You follow it room to room, ear to the faded wallpaper, until it stops at the front hall, at a glass trophy case nobody in the house will look at. Inside are sleeping bags, a diary with a broken lock, a coffee can of curlers. On the inside of the glass are sawdust fingerprints. At your feet lies a pink foam curler that was not there a minute ago, still warm.
success.art: A teenager with an ear pressed to old floral wallpaper beside a glowing glass trophy case of sleeping bags, diaries and hair curlers, sawdust fingerprints on the inside of the glass, a pink foam curler on the floorboards

failure.text: A drill bit punches through the wallpaper an inch from your ear, whirs, and withdraws, leaving a neat round hole and a puff of plaster dust on your shoulder. Through the hole, a girl's voice says, quite calmly, "Wrong room."
failure.art: A spinning drill bit punching through floral wallpaper in a dim hallway, a puff of plaster dust, a startled teenager pressed against the opposite wall across the hallway

choices.label: Take a candle down to the cellar fuse box, and do not say you'll be right back

success.text: Every fuse in the box has a tiny, perfect hole drilled through its glass. You swap in spares from a coffee can and the house blazes back to light. On the cellar workbench, somebody has sorted the brothers' jumbled junk drawer into jars by size: wood screws, washers, wing nuts, the way a shop teacher would. A note in block capitals is taped to the last jar: LABEL YOUR HARDWARE, BOYS.
success.art: A teenager by candlelight replacing glass fuses in an old cellar fuse box, a workbench behind them lined with neatly sorted jars of screws and washers

failure.text: Halfway down the cellar stairs the door swings shut behind you, and you hear four screws go into the jamb, one by one, unhurried. It takes Moose twenty minutes and a butter knife to take the door off its hinges. You spend all twenty sitting on the stairs in the dark, listening to someone hum.
failure.art: A teenager sitting alone on dark cellar stairs clutching a guttering candle, the door above them screwed shut, a sliver of light underneath it

signature.title: The Line Is Dead
signature.place: The Gamma Rho house in a thunderstorm, midnight
signature.text: Rain hammers the old house. Somebody tries to order a pizza and the phone in the hall has no dial tone, only a hiss, and under the hiss a drill, far off, then close. Reggie checks the front door: screws, a whole row of them, driven in from outside. The back door: screws. Every window has a sheet of plywood over it that was not there at dinner. Chad, in pink foam curlers and a cold-cream face, whispers, "This is the part in the movie where the phone rings and it's coming from inside the house." The phone rings.
signature.art: A dark Victorian front hall at midnight during a thunderstorm, a gangly young man in pink foam curlers and white cold cream holding a ringing black rotary phone receiver out to a teenager, young men in half-finished drag staring at the front door lined with a row of screw heads, plywood screwed over every window, white lightning flashing through the cracks, candle and flashlight light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Take the receiver from Chad and answer it

success.text: Through the static a girl's voice says, "Valley State switchboard. Who are you calling?" You ask if this is Dot. A long silence. "Nobody's called me that since sixty-six." You ask what she wants. "Tell them to give it back," she says. "Tell them to say it. They know what it is." The line clicks. In the morning every window is clear again, a neat ring of screw holes around each one.
success.art: A teenager holding an old rotary phone receiver to their ear in a dark hallway lit by lightning, brothers in curlers and cold cream huddled close, the cord crackling with faint amber light

failure.text: The receiver goes hot in your hand and the drill screams down the line so loud the brothers cover their ears. When it stops, the cord has been neatly cut, and a voice is still coming out of the earpiece anyway: "Harmless fun. Harmless fun. Harmless fun."
failure.art: A teenager holding a smoking phone receiver at arm's length in a dark hallway, the cut cord dangling, young men in curlers and cold cream covering their ears

choices.label: Back the screws out of the kitchen door with a dime: lefty loosey

success.text: Thirty-one screws. You count them out loud, and by the twentieth Teddy is counting with you and Reggie is holding the flashlight. The kitchen door swings open on the wet night. Out on the lawn, in the rain, a figure in curlers watches you from the trees, then holds up one finger, like a teacher marking a correct answer, and walks back into the pines.
success.art: A teenager turning screws out of a kitchen door with a dime by flashlight, a young man in a wig counting along, the door swinging open onto a rainy lawn where a figure in coveralls and curlers stands at the edge of dark pines

failure.text: The dime snaps. Behind you, something drills in a new screw for every one you take out, always one step ahead, with a soft, patient whir. By dawn the kitchen door has more screws in it than wood.
failure.art: A kitchen door at dawn studded with dozens of screws in tidy rows, a snapped dime on the linoleum, an exhausted teenager slumped against the cabinets

choices.label: Gather everyone in one room with every flashlight you own

success.text: Zelda's rules: never split up, never go upstairs, never investigate the noise. The whole house crams into the parlor in sequins, curlers and bathrobes, every flashlight pointed at the door. The drilling circles the house twice, slow, and stops outside the parlor window. Then it moves on. Nobody sleeps, but everybody is there at breakfast.
success.art: A crowd of young men in sequins, curlers and bathrobes crammed into one parlor clutching flashlights pointed at the door, a stormy window behind them glowing amber from outside

failure.text: Somebody always needs the bathroom. Teddy goes. Teddy comes back, white as a sheet, with one perfect hole drilled through the heel of each of his shoes, and will not say a word about what he saw in the upstairs hall.
failure.art: A pale young man in a bathrobe holding up a pair of high heels with neat round holes drilled through each heel, brothers in curlers staring at him by flashlight

signature.title: The Heel Snaps
signature.place: The shortcut through the quarry pines, Old Quarry Road, 11 p.m.
signature.text: You are walking Chad home from a costume fitting at the Glitter Box along the shortcut through the quarry pines. He insisted on wearing the pumps, because Glory says you have to break them in, and he is wearing the wig, because it would not fit in the bag. The wind picks up. A flashlight beam flickers between the trees behind you. Then the whine of a drill, low and steady, and getting closer. Chad walks faster. Then: snap. His left heel goes, and he goes down in the pine needles, and his towering blond wig catches on a low branch and hangs there like a flag of surrender. "Go on without me!" he sobs, mascara running. "Tell Glory I nailed the walk!" The beam swings toward you both.
signature.art: A dark pine forest shortcut at eleven at night, a gangly young man in a sequined gown sprawled in the pine needles clutching a snapped high heel with mascara running down his cheeks, a towering blond wig dangling from a low branch above him, a teenager kneeling beside him, and a flashlight beam cutting between the trees behind them, wind in the pines, blue moonlight and white beam, wide shot

choices.label: Kick off your sneakers and swap with Chad

success.text: You hobble in one pump, he runs in your sneakers, and you make it to the porch together, laughing and crying. At the edge of the trees the beam stops on his snapped heel, then on the wig still hanging from its branch. In the morning both are on the Gamma Rho welcome mat: the wig combed out, the heel glued back on and held tight in a little C-clamp to dry.
success.art: A front porch at dawn with a combed-out blond wig and a high heel glued and held in a small C-clamp on the welcome mat, wet pine needles on the steps

failure.text: Your sneakers are three sizes too small for him. You both go down in a heap. The flashlight beam stands over you, holding steady, and the drill revs once, twice, close enough to feel. Then the beam just stays on you, all the way back to the house, never closer and never farther, so you will feel it.
failure.art: A teenager and a young man in a sequined gown tangled together in pine needles under a hard flashlight beam, dark pines all around

choices.label: Snap off his other heel so he can run flat

success.text: You grab his right pump and crack the heel off against a tree. Flats! Chad takes off like a deer in sequins, and you yank the wig off its branch on the way past. You burst into the Gamma Rho kitchen together, gasping. Glory, waiting up, looks at the shoes. "Resourceful," she says. "Mother approves."
success.art: A young man in a sequined gown sprinting through moonlit pines in broken-heeled shoes, a teenager running beside him clutching a blond wig, a flashlight beam far behind

failure.text: The heel will not snap. Chad limps, you half carry him, and the wig stays behind on its branch. Glancing back, you see a hand in a canvas work glove reach out of the dark and lift it carefully off the twig. You run the rest of the way.
failure.art: A hand in a canvas work glove lifting a blond wig off a pine branch in the dark, a teenager and a limping young man in a gown fleeing in the background

choices.label: Haul Chad onto your back and run for the house

success.text: Chad is six-foot-three before the heels and you carry him anyway, gown flapping, his arms around your neck, both of you screaming the whole way. You crash through the back door into the kitchen, and Moose catches you both. Out in the pines, the drill stops whining. It almost sounds like someone laughing.
success.alone: Chad is six-foot-three before the heels and you carry him anyway, gown flapping, his arms around your neck, both of you screaming the whole way. You crash through the back door and the two of you land in a heap on the kitchen linoleum. Out in the pines, the drill stops whining. It almost sounds like someone laughing.
success.art: A teenager running through dark pines carrying a much taller young man in a sequined gown piggyback, his heels kicking, both screaming, a gentle giant holding open a lit kitchen door ahead

failure.text: Three steps and your knees buckle. You both tumble down a pine slope into a drainage ditch full of cold water. You crawl out filthy and freezing, and on the rim of the ditch sits a neat little stack: Chad's snapped heel and three drywall screws.
failure.art: A teenager and a young man in a soaked sequined gown climbing out of a muddy drainage ditch at night, a snapped high heel and three screws set neatly on the rim above them

signature.title: I'll Be Right Back
signature.place: The Gamma Rho house in a blackout, 1 a.m.
signature.text: The power is out again. Ten brothers sit in a candlelit circle on the parlor floor, and Chad, in his full Lady Chadelier gown and a fresh coat of lipstick that has smeared in the panic, stands up. "My lipstick is a disaster. I'm going to go fix it." He picks up a candle. "I'll be right back." Every person in the room screams "NO!" at once. He is already gone, and not out the front door to the street. Up the stairs. From somewhere above comes the slow, patient whine of a drill.
signature.art: A candlelit Victorian parlor during a blackout at one in the morning, ten young men in gowns and wigs sitting in a circle on the floor with their mouths open mid-scream, and a gangly young man in a towering blond wig, a long sequined gown and smeared red lipstick climbing a dark staircase holding a single candle, the top of the stairs lost in shadow, warm candlelight and black shadows, wide shot

choices.label: Grab a brother's hand and go up after Chad together

success.text: You find him in the upstairs bathroom, reapplying Fire Engine Fantasy by candlelight, frozen. In the mirror, behind him, stands Dot, curlers and goggles, drill hanging at her side, staring at his reflection. Chad, shaking, holds the lipstick up over his shoulder. "It's, um, it's very forgiving," he squeaks. She looks at the tube for a long time, puzzled, as if no boy in this house has ever offered her anything before. Then she is gone.
success.art: A young man in a towering blond wig holding a lipstick tube over his shoulder toward a bathroom mirror, the reflection of a translucent girl in coveralls and pink curlers behind him by candlelight, a teenager and a young man in a wig holding hands in the doorway

failure.text: Your brother lets go on the landing. You reach the bathroom alone and it is empty, the candle still burning on the sink and the mirror drilled full of tiny holes that spell out nothing at all. Chad turns up at dawn asleep in the clawfoot bathtub, wrapped in the shower curtain like a burrito, and remembers none of it.
failure.art: A lone teenager in a candlelit bathroom staring at a mirror peppered with neat drill holes, a guttering candle on the sink, a shower curtain drawn around a clawfoot tub

choices.label: Get everyone out to Reggie's station wagon and make it start

success.text: Of course it will not start. You pop the hood: the distributor cap has a hole drilled clean through it. You plug it with a wad of Chad's chewing gum and a bobby pin from his wig, and the engine coughs, then roars. In the headlights a lanky figure in goggles stands in the driveway. She tilts her head at the gum, nods once, like that was a passing grade, and steps aside.
success.art: A teenager under the raised hood of an old station wagon at night patching an engine part with gum and a bobby pin, young men in wigs piled in the back seat, the headlights blazing on a translucent figure in goggles and blue coveralls stepping aside in the driveway

failure.text: The engine turns over, and over, and over. Every brother is in the car in full drag, Chad in the back screaming "DRIVE!", and the headlights flick on by themselves to show the shop girl standing at the hood, tapping her drill against the grille. Everybody runs back into the house, which is worse.
failure.art: Young men in wigs and gowns piling out of a stalled station wagon and running toward a dark Victorian house, headlights lighting a translucent girl in coveralls at the hood with an old drill

choices.label: Bellow the Final Girl Rules up the stairwell

success.text: "NEVER SPLIT UP! NEVER GO UPSTAIRS! NEVER SAY YOU'LL BE RIGHT BACK!" From above, Chad wails, "I ALREADY SAID IT!" "THEN COME BACK DOWN AND UNSAY IT!" A pause. Then he comes clattering down the stairs in one shoe, and this time he goes out the front door to the porch, the right way. The drill above stops, as if it is grading him.
success.art: A teenager with cupped hands shouting up a dark stairwell, a young man in a blond wig and gown clattering down the stairs in one shoe toward an open front door and the porch

failure.text: Your voice cracks on "upstairs." Chad, panicking, does the only thing he can think of and goes farther up, into the attic. You find him there an hour later, barricaded behind a pile of moth-eaten sleeping bags, clutching his wig like a teddy bear.
failure.art: A young man in a gown barricaded behind a heap of old sleeping bags in a dusty attic by candlelight, hugging a blond wig, a teenager peering up through the trapdoor

signature.title: The Trophy Case
signature.place: The Gamma Rho front hall, the night before Halloween
signature.text: The trophy case is glowing. Inside, behind the glass, are eighteen Halloweens of other people's things, each with a brass plate: RAID 1951, RAID 1958, RAID 1963. A pink sleeping bag. A diary with its little lock pried off. Spare flannel pajamas from somebody's overnight bag, folded small. A coffee can of foam curlers. And in the center, pinned to faded velvet, a blue ribbon: FIRST PLACE, INDUSTRIAL ARTS, 1966. The glass is covered in drill holes, hundreds of them, in perfect circles, not one finished. On the stairs, Dot sits with the drill across her knees, waiting. "Go on," Dot Ruskin says. "Open it. Twenty years, and nobody in this house ever wanted to."
signature.art: A dim Victorian front hall the night before Halloween, a glowing glass trophy case holding a pink sleeping bag, a small diary with its lock pried off, folded flannel pajamas, a coffee can of foam curlers and a blue ribbon pinned to faded velvet, the glass covered in hundreds of small round drill holes, and on the stairs a lanky freckled translucent teenage girl in oil-stained blue coveralls over red plaid pajamas, pink foam curlers and round amber goggles sitting with an old chrome drill across her knees, a teenager facing her, warm case glow, medium wide shot

choices.label: Pick the case's lock with a bobby pin from Chad's wig

success.text: The little lock clicks. You lift out the blue ribbon and hold it out to her. Dot stands. She crosses the hall slowly and takes it in her work-gloved hand, and for the first time all week, the drill in her other hand stops whining completely. In the silence you can hear her breathe. "First place," she says. "I did the dovetails by hand."
success.art: A teenager holding out a blue ribbon to a translucent girl in coveralls and pink curlers in a dim hallway, her gloved hand reaching for it, an old drill hanging silent at her side, a glass trophy case standing open behind them

failure.text: The bobby pin bends. The lock bites it in half. Dot sighs, the drill revs, and every brass plate in the case rattles like teeth. "They always said they'd fix it later," she says, and walks up the stairs into the long dark hallway.
failure.art: A teenager kneeling at a glass trophy case with a broken bobby pin, brass plates rattling inside, a flickering teenage girl in oil-stained blue work clothes walking away up a long dark staircase

choices.label: Read every brass plate out loud, year by year

success.text: "Raid, 1949." Your voice echoes. "Raid, 1950." Brothers come out of their rooms in wigs and robes to listen. By 1960, Reggie is reading with you. By 1966 he has to stop, because his voice is shaking. Dot listens to all eighteen with her eyes closed. "Somebody finally said it out loud," she says, "like it counted."
success.art: A teenager reading brass plates aloud at a glowing trophy case, young men in wigs and bathrobes gathered on the stairs to listen, a translucent girl in coveralls listening with her eyes closed

failure.text: Halfway through, the plates start reading themselves back to you in boys' voices, laughing, whooping, the way they sounded in the yard. You cannot hear yourself over them. When it stops, Dot is gone and the case is darker than before.
failure.art: A teenager covering their ears in front of a trophy case whose brass plates glow and rattle, ghostly laughing young men in rubber monster masks reflected in the glass

choices.label: Get Reggie, the house president, to face her and say sorry

success.text: Reggie comes down in his gold gown with his wig in his hands. He has never been in the room with her before. "I didn't know," he says. "That's not good enough. I walked past this case every day and never asked whose things they were. I'm sorry. The house is sorry." Dot looks at him a long time. "First time anybody from this house has said that word," she says. "Say it again tomorrow. Louder."
success.art: A young man in a gold gown holding his wig in both hands, apologizing to a translucent figure in goggles and blue coveralls and curlers seated on a staircase, a glowing glass trophy case between them, a teenager standing beside him

failure.text: Reggie gets as far as "I'm," and the drill shrieks and the words fall apart. He runs back upstairs, ashamed. Dot watches him go. "All this time," she says, "and still nobody can finish the sentence."
failure.art: A young man in a gold gown fleeing up a dark staircase, a translucent girl in coveralls with a revving drill watching him go, a glowing trophy case in the hall

signature.title: The Workbench
signature.place: The Gamma Rho cellar, which is a 1966 shop room, 2 a.m.
signature.text: You go down to the cellar for the spare fuses and walk into 1966. The cellar is a high-school shop room now: workbenches, iron vises, a pegboard of painted tool outlines, sawdust in the lamplight. At the oldest bench, Dot Ruskin is sanding a cedar hope chest, the same corner over and over, curlers bobbing. A man's voice crackles from a speaker on the wall: "Miss Ruskin, home economics is down the hall." She does not look up. "I know where it is," she says. Then she looks at you, goggles up, face to face for the first time. "You lost?"
signature.art: A cellar transformed into a 1966 high school shop room at two in the morning, wooden workbenches, iron vises, a pegboard of painted tool outlines, sawdust in the air under a hanging lamp, a lanky freckled translucent teenage girl in oil-stained blue coveralls over red plaid pajamas with pink foam curlers sanding the corner of a cedar hope chest, amber goggles pushed up, looking up at a teenager standing on the cellar stairs, warm lamp light, medium shot

choices.label: Pull up a stool and ask her to show you how

success.text: She considers you, then slides a scrap of pine across the bench. "Let the tool do the work. Don't push." She shows you how to hold her father's drill, steady, two hands, and you drill one clean pilot hole while she watches. Dot almost smiles. "Huh. Nobody ever asked me to show them anything."
success.art: A teenager carefully drilling a pilot hole in a scrap of pine at a shop workbench under a hanging lamp, a see-through shop-class girl in grease-stained overalls and curlers leaning in to point at the wood, sawdust floating in the light

failure.text: You reach for the drill before she offers it, and her face shuts like a lid. "That's mine. That was my dad's." The lamp swings, the pegboard rattles, and you are back in an ordinary cellar full of empty soda cans and old lawn chairs, with sawdust in your hair.
failure.art: A teenager alone in a cluttered ordinary cellar under a swinging bare bulb, sawdust in their hair, a bare pegboard rattling on the wall

choices.label: Hand her the clamp she's reaching for, before she asks

success.text: You read the joint, see what she needs, and set the bar clamp in her hand. She tightens it without looking, then stops, and looks. "In two years of shop," she says, "nobody ever handed me anything. They'd watch me reach." She lets you hold the other end of the chest while the glue sets.
success.art: A teenager passing a wooden bar clamp to a translucent girl in coveralls at a workbench, both holding a cedar chest steady together under lamplight

failure.text: You hand her the wrong clamp. She laughs, not unkindly, and the room flickers between 1966 and 1986 so fast it makes you sick. You climb the cellar stairs dizzy and find the door screwed shut, with one screw left loose, as a hint.
failure.art: A dizzy teenager climbing cellar stairs toward a door lined with screws, the cellar below flickering between an old shop room and a cluttered basement

choices.label: Yank the drill's frayed cord out of the wall

success.text: The cord rips out of the socket with a blue spark and the drill dies in her hands. Silence. Dot stares at you. "That's what Mr. Gault did," she says quietly. "Pulled my plug in front of the whole class." But she lets you go up the stairs, and the house stays lit all night.
success.art: A teenager holding a frayed electrical cord yanked from a sparking wall socket in a cellar shop room, a flickering teenage girl in oil-stained blue work clothes staring at them with a silent drill in her hands

failure.text: The cord whips out of your hand like a snake, and every light in the house goes out at once. In the pitch black you hear her plug it back in, and the whine starts again, closer. You find the stairs by touch.
failure.art: A pitch-dark cellar lit only by the amber glow of safety goggles and a frayed cord sparking against a wall socket, a teenager groping for the stairs

signature.title: It's Just a Joke, Man
signature.text: All rehearsal, Trip Thurston has been filming the brothers on his camcorder "for the guys at State," zooming in on Chad's wobbling walk for laughs, then panning to the trophy case and tapping the glass. "Harmless fun, man. My dad's year is in there. Boys will be boys. It's just a joke." He won't touch a wig either, but that isn't what makes the room go cold. Glory tells him the only joke in the house is his attitude. He storms out to sit in his convertible. Through the parlor window you watch the dome light flicker. The drill whines. One by one, screws go into the car doors from outside, and then the dome light goes out. When you get there the convertible is empty, its doors screwed shut, the camcorder on the seat still recording, and the front door of the house is standing open on an upstairs hallway that runs far, far too long.
signature.art: A white convertible parked in a dark gravel driveway at midnight with its doors studded with fresh screws driven in from outside, an empty driver's seat with a camcorder lying on it with its small red light glowing, a teenager running up to the car, and behind it an old Victorian house with its front door standing open on a staircase rising into an impossibly long glowing hallway, porch light and blue night, wide shot

choices.label: Fish the camcorder out through the vent window and play back the tape

success.text: On the tiny screen: Trip laughing at himself in the rearview mirror. Then a girl in coveralls over plaid pajamas, pink curlers, goggles, standing calmly by his window. "You've got something of ours," she says. The doors are open again. She walks him up the porch steps and into the house, and he goes without a word, the way the girls went out into the yard. The last shot is the trophy case.
success.art: A teenager in a dark driveway watching the tiny glowing screen of a camcorder showing a translucent girl in coveralls and pink curlers leading a young man up porch steps, a convertible with screwed-shut doors behind them

failure.text: The tape is all static and the scream of a drill, then a girl's voice, flat and tired: "Boys will be boys." The cassette door pops open and the tape unspools itself across the driveway like a long brown ribbon.
failure.art: Brown videotape spilling out of a camcorder and unspooling across a dark driveway in the wind, a startled teenager holding the camera

choices.label: Run straight up the stairs after him

success.text: The hallway stretches as you run, doors and doors and doors. At the far end, in a flashlight beam on the cold floor, Trip sits in a sleeping bag, alone, shivering, while somewhere boys laugh. You get close enough to hear him: "It wasn't me. It was my dad." Then the hall snaps back like a rubber band and you are standing at the top of ordinary stairs.
success.art: An impossibly long Victorian upstairs hallway of identical doors, a young man shivering alone in a sleeping bag in a flashlight beam at the far end, a teenager running toward him

failure.text: The stairs keep going up. You climb for what feels like an hour, past the attic, past the roof, and come out, gasping, through your own front door at dawn, on Crystal Street, two miles away.
failure.art: An endless dark staircase spiraling upward past many landings, a tiny exhausted teenager climbing, a faint glow of dawn at the very top

choices.label: Get every brother into the parlor, together, lights on

success.text: They come, wigs askew, in sequins and sweatpants. Reggie takes a hand, Teddy takes another, and Chad takes the last one, his lipstick perfect. "Nobody goes anywhere alone," Reggie says. Glory nods. "And nobody says it's just a joke." All night the whine circles the house, past every window, but it never stops at the parlor. The ones who are in it, it leaves alone.
success.art: Young men in sequins, sweatpants and crooked wigs holding hands in a lit parlor, a drag queen standing with them, a flashlight beam sliding past the dark windows outside

failure.text: The brothers argue about calling the police. The phone is dead. Teddy says he will just run out and get his car keys and he'll be right back. Everyone screams. He comes back laughing too loudly, holding up his key ring: every key on it has a neat round hole drilled through the middle, and a pink foam curler is hooked on the ring.
failure.art: A young man in a wig in a parlor doorway holding up a key ring where every key has a round hole drilled through it and a pink foam curler dangles from the ring, brothers in sequins and sweatpants staring

signature.title: The Siege
signature.place: The Gamma Rho front door, 3 a.m.
signature.text: The drill is coming through the front door. A ring of holes is going in around the lock, one by one, each with a puff of sawdust, slow as a clock. Inside, a dozen brothers in half-finished drag, sequins and sweatpants, one false eyelash each, shove the parlor couch against the door. The trophy case glows behind them. Chad, in his wig and a fuzzy robe, is holding a curling iron like a baseball bat. "I am a damsel," he announces, voice trembling, "and I am NOT in distress." The fifth hole goes in. Then the sixth.
signature.art: The inside of a Victorian front door at three in the morning, a ring of fresh drill holes appearing around the lock with puffs of sawdust blowing inward, young men in sequins, sweatpants and wigs with single false eyelashes bracing a heavy couch against the door, a gangly young man in a towering blond wig and a fuzzy pink robe gripping a curling iron in both hands over his shoulder, a glowing glass trophy case behind them, warm lamp light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Brace the door shoulder to shoulder with every brother in heels

success.text: "On three!" Reggie shouts. Every brother puts a shoulder to the door, heels skidding on the floorboards, wigs slipping, nobody letting go. The drilling stops. Through one of the holes, an eye in an amber safety goggle peers in at a line of boys in sequins holding a door together with their whole bodies. She looks for a long time. Then her footsteps go down the porch steps.
success.art: A line of young men in sequined gowns and wigs bracing a front door together with their shoulders, heels skidding on floorboards, an amber-glowing goggled eye peering in through a drill hole

failure.text: The ring of holes closes. The lock drops out and clatters on the floor. The door swings open on an empty porch, a scatter of sawdust, a single pink curler. Half the brothers scream and run upstairs instead of out, and you spend an hour finding them in closets.
failure.art: An open front door with its lock fallen out onto the floor, sawdust and a pink curler on an empty moonlit porch, young men in wigs fleeing up a staircase behind

choices.label: Slide one stolen diary out to her through the drill holes

success.text: You take the house key ring off its hook, unlock the case, and pull out a little diary marked RAID 1966. You roll it tight and push it out through the biggest hole. The drill stops. A long pause. A soft voice on the other side: "That's Marjorie's. She cried for a week. She thought they'd read it out loud at their parties." Then quietly, so quietly: "Thank you." The drilling does not start again.
success.art: A teenager pushing a small rolled diary through a drill hole in a front door, a key ring hanging from an open trophy case behind them, a gloved hand taking the diary from the other side

failure.text: You grab the house key ring off its hook, but none of the keys fit. The little case key went missing with Trip, the brother who vanished upstairs on the first night. You rattle the glass. The drilling speeds up.
failure.art: A teenager rattling a key ring at the locked door of a glowing glass trophy case while drill holes multiply around a front door lock behind them

choices.label: Blast a can of Aqua-Glow through the holes

success.text: A shimmering cloud billows out through the holes. On the porch, someone coughs, then sneezes, then mutters, "Oh, for Pete's sake." Through the peephole you watch a lanky figure in curlers wiping her goggles on her pajama sleeve, thoroughly annoyed, retreating into the trees to wait it out.
success.art: A shimmering cloud of hairspray billowing out of drill holes onto a moonlit porch, a translucent figure in goggles and blue coveralls and curlers wiping her goggles on her sleeve, retreating toward dark pines

failure.text: Blowback. The cloud comes right back through the holes into your face. Your eyes stream, the brothers cough, and every wig in the room is stuck at a new and terrible angle. The drilling never even slowed down.
failure.art: A teenager coughing in a glittering cloud of hairspray beside a drilled front door, young men around them with wigs stuck at wild angles, eyes streaming

signature.title: Final Dress
signature.place: The Glitter Box Playhouse, the night before Halloween, 11 p.m.
signature.text: The last dress rehearsal before drag night, on the Glitter Box stage between the rain buckets. Glory is in the front row with a clipboard and a box of tissues. Chad is mid-number as Lady Chadelier, lip-syncing to Cher in a gown Moose hemmed by hand, giving it everything. Then every stage light dies at once. In the dark, the old follow spot in the back booth clicks on by itself, swings across the house, and pins Chad dead center in a circle of hard white light. Up in the booth, two amber goggles glow. Chad freezes, one arm still raised to the balcony.
signature.art: A dark theater stage dotted with rain buckets at eleven at night, a gangly young man in a towering blond wig and a hand-hemmed sequined gown frozen mid-performance with one arm raised, pinned in a single hard circle of white follow-spot light, a tall drag queen in the front row with a clipboard and a box of tissues, and high in the back booth two round amber goggles glowing in the dark, wide shot

choices.label: Yell to Chad to finish the number, right into her light

success.text: "Finish it, Chadelier!" Glory roars. Chad takes a breath and does. Every step, every lip, the big arm on the last note, straight up into the light. And the spot holds on him, steady and smooth, following each turn the way only somebody who knows exactly what she is doing can run a light. When he hits the final pose, the spot irises down slowly, perfectly, to black. Glory is crying. "She gave him his light," she whispers. "Honey, she gave him his light."
success.art: A young man in a towering blond wig and sequined gown hitting a triumphant final pose in a perfect follow-spot circle, a drag queen weeping in the front row, two amber goggles glowing in the booth high above

failure.text: Chad bolts offstage, and the spot follows him everywhere, into the wings, the dressing room, the alley, a hard white circle he cannot get out of, until he is crouched behind the dumpster with his face in his hands.
failure.art: A young man in a sequined gown and blond wig crouched behind an alley dumpster with his face in his hands, pinned in a hard circle of white light from a high theatre window

choices.label: Climb up to the booth and stand beside her

success.text: Dot is at the follow spot, both hands on the handles, curlers bobbing. She does not stop running it when you come in. "Your boy's got nerve," she says. "Bad footwork. Good nerve." Below, Glory calls up into the dark: "Dorothy Ruskin! You fixed that light for me in sixty-six!" Dot's hands go still on the handles. "She remembers," she says, very quietly.
success.art: A translucent girl in coveralls and pink curlers running an old follow spot in a cramped theatre booth, a teenager beside her, the bright stage far below with a performer in a blond wig and a drag queen calling up from the seats

failure.text: The booth ladder whirs, every rung turning loose in your hands. You hang off the catwalk while the spot sweeps the seats looking for you. Frankie hauls you down with a rope and a string of words Glory pretends not to hear.
failure.art: A teenager dangling from a theatre catwalk by their hands, a follow spot beam sweeping the empty seats below, a stage manager in a headset hauling on a rope

choices.label: Get to the lighting board and bring the stage lights back up

success.text: The board is a 1960s monster of sliders, and someone has labeled every one in neat block capitals on masking tape, decades ago. You bring the warm lights up slowly, a sunrise across the stage, and the follow spot dims to match them instead of fighting them. In the booth, the goggles blink once, approving.
success.art: A teenager sliding up the faders on an old theatre lighting board by flashlight, a warm wash of light spreading across a stage, a follow spot dimming in a booth above

failure.text: You shove the wrong slider and every light in the Glitter Box flares and blows at once in a shower of sparks. The rain buckets hiss. In the dark, the drill whines from the booth, sounding, for the first time, genuinely offended.
failure.art: Theatre stage lights bursting in a shower of sparks above a rain-bucket-strewn stage, a teenager at a lighting board shielding their face

finale.title: Drag Night
finale.place: The Gamma Rho house, Halloween night
finale.text: Halloween night, and the Gamma Rho parlor is packed: Crystal Street kids in costumes, a few brave parents, a jar for the Glitter Box roof already half full. Glory Hallelujah emcees in silver sequins on a stage of card tables. The brothers are ready in full drag, wigs pinned, heels on, Lady Chadelier in front, terrified and radiant. At the stroke of midnight every light dies. Every door and window in the house screws itself shut from the outside, a hundred drills at once. The staircase stretches up into an endless glowing hallway, and down it comes Dot Ruskin, coveralls over plaid pajamas, curlers, goggles glowing, her father's drill revving, its cord running up into the dark where Trip Thurston, the brother who called it all a joke, vanished on the first night. "Eighteen Halloweens in a glass box," she says, "and you called it fun. They called me dangerous. Give it back. Say it. Or nobody leaves this house until every one of you knows how that cold yard felt."
finale.art: A packed Victorian parlor on Halloween night, kids in costumes and a few parents crowded around a folding-table stage, young men in full drag with wigs and heels lined up in front, a tall drag queen emcee in silver sequins, every window crossed with screwed-on planks, and coming down a staircase that rises into an endless glowing hallway a lanky freckled translucent teenage girl in oil-stained blue coveralls over red plaid pajamas, pink foam curlers and glowing amber goggles holding an old chrome drill with its cord trailing up into the dark, four teenagers in costumes at the foot of the stairs, wide shot

choices.label: Charge the stairs and wrench the drill out of her hands

success.text: You take the stairs three at a time and grab the drill with both hands. It bucks like a live thing, but you twist, and it comes free of her grip, the cord tearing loose in a shower of blue sparks. The hallway snaps shut. Dot flickers like a bad bulb, and is gone. Every screw in the house backs itself out and drops to the floor at once, a hundred tiny bells. Trip comes stumbling down the stairs in a sleeping bag, and nobody ever explains anything.
success.art: A teenager on a Victorian staircase holding an old chrome drill high by its handle, its frayed cord torn loose in blue sparks, a flickering translucent girl in coveralls and curlers one step above, screws raining from boarded windows

failure.text: She has had twenty years to get a grip on that drill. She plants a boot, turns it in one slow circle, and the banister you were holding comes apart post by post, every spindle unscrewed and laid neatly beside you on the stairs. "Lefty loosey," she says. The hallway gets longer.
failure.art: A teenager sitting dazed on a staircase beside a neat row of unscrewed banister spindles, a flickering teenage girl in oil-stained blue work clothes standing on the landing above with an old drill raised toward the ceiling

choices.label: Kill the main breaker: her drill runs on the house's own current

success.text: Her cord finds an outlet in every room, so you take the outlets away. You slip through the crowd to the basement panel and throw the main. The drill whines down and dies. Dot looks at it, betrayed, shakes it, and in the dark she fades with it, dimming like a filament. When the lights come back, the doors are unlocked and the staircase is just a staircase.
success.art: A teenager throwing a big main breaker lever in a dark basement, upstairs a translucent girl in coveralls fading like a cooling filament as the drill in her hands winds down

failure.text: You throw the main. Nothing happens. The drill keeps running: the cord has jumped to the outlet upstairs, in the hallway, in the dark. "Wrong outlet," Dot says, and the whole house hums.
failure.art: A teenager staring at a thrown breaker in a pitch-dark basement while above, a frayed cord glows and hums its way up a staircase into a long dark hallway

choices.label: Make the house give back every trophy, say sorry out loud, and pin on her ribbon

success.text: You hold up the Clarion clipping, the crossed-out judging sheet, the list she wrote in the booth. "You drilled a trunk lock to get your friends' things back," you say. "That's all. And they called it harmless fun when the boys did worse." Then Reggie unlocks the case. One by one, every brother in full drag carries a trophy across the parlor and lays it at the foot of the stairs: Marjorie's diary, Linda's sleeping bag, Pat's curlers, eighteen Halloweens of other people's things. "It wasn't harmless," Reggie says, "and it wasn't fun, and it was never your fault. We're sorry." The whole house says it with him. You pin the blue ribbon on her coveralls. Glory steps forward. "And Miss Ruskin, my stage needs building, and I've never had a better hand on my lights." The drill winds down to silence in Dot's hand. She looks down at the ribbon, and at the pile of returned things, and for the first time since 1966, she cries.
success.art: Young men in sequined gowns and wigs laying sleeping bags, diaries and coffee cans of curlers at the foot of a staircase, a teenager pinning a blue ribbon on a translucent figure in goggles and blue coveralls and pink curlers, a drag queen in silver sequins holding out her hand, an old drill hanging silent at the girl's side

failure.text: You try, but the brothers hesitate at the case, looking at each other, and the hesitation is all Dot needs to see. "You still have to think about it," she says. The drill revs. You have the whole truth in your hands, and the house is not ready to say it yet.
failure.art: Young men in gowns and wigs hesitating before an open glowing trophy case, a translucent girl in coveralls on the stairs turning away with a revving drill, a teenager holding old papers

choices.label: Drop the needle and start the show in the dark, the way those first rehearsals taught you

success.text: Those first rehearsals taught you how Dot works: she stops for anyone who keeps going, she fixes what breaks, and she only takes the ones who laugh. So you drop the needle on the record and shout "WALK!" and the brothers walk, in the pitch dark, in full drag, one after another down the card-table runway, while the whole parlor whoops for them. The drill falters. Dot sits down on the stairs to watch, chin on her fist, and stays through every number, all the way to the last bow, and when the sun comes up through the boarded windows, the screws drop out and she is gone.
success.art: Young men in full drag strutting down a card-table runway in a dark parlor lit by flashlights while costumed kids cheer, a see-through shop-class girl in grease-stained overalls and curlers sitting on the stairs with her chin on her fist, watching, dawn creeping through boarded windows

failure.text: The needle skips. The brothers stumble in the dark. Dot watches one shaky step and shakes her head. "Not tonight," she says. "A show's not enough. Not without the two words."
failure.art: A record player skipping in a dark parlor, young men in drag stumbling on a card-table runway, a translucent girl on the stairs shaking her head

choices.label: Line the brothers up shoulder to shoulder in their heels and hold the stairs, the way they stopped running midweek

success.text: Midweek you watched these boys stop running: they held doors, held hands, held the line. So you line them up again, at the foot of the stairs, arms linked, heels planted, wigs pinned, the whole parlor behind them. Dot comes down with the drill shrieking. They do not break. She pushes, and they hold. She pushes harder, and Chad, in front, holds hardest of all. The drill whines down to a sputter, and Dot backs up the stairs, step by step, into the hallway, until the hallway folds shut behind her like a closing book and every screw in the house drops out.
success.art: A wall of young men in sequined gowns and wigs linking arms at the foot of a staircase, heels planted, a translucent girl in coveralls backing up the stairs into a closing hallway as her drill sputters, screws raining from boarded windows

failure.text: Someone's heel skids. The line buckles, and the brothers fall back in a heap of sequins. "Huh," she says. "I've seen dovetails hold better."
failure.art: A heap of young men in sequins and wigs tumbled together at the foot of a staircase, a flickering teenage girl in oil-stained blue work clothes standing on the landing above them with an old drill held at her side

choices.label: Hand her the ribbon again in front of the whole house, and give her the workbench

success.text: The night before Halloween you met her face to face, at the trophy case, at the workbench, in the lighting booth, and learned what she was really after: not revenge, but her things, two words and a place at the bench. So you give her all three, in front of everyone. Reggie unlocks the case and the brothers carry back every trophy, eighteen Halloweens of it, and lay it at her boots, and the whole house says sorry, out loud, together. You pin the blue ribbon on her coveralls. Glory takes her by the work-gloved hand. "The stage needs building, Miss Ruskin. The bench is yours." Dot looks at the ribbon and the pile of things that finally came home, and the drill goes silent in her hand.
success.art: Young men in sequined gowns laying sleeping bags, diaries and curlers at the boots of a translucent girl in coveralls wearing a blue ribbon, a drag queen in silver sequins holding her gloved hand, a teenager beside them, a silent old drill at her side

failure.text: She reaches for the ribbon, then pulls back. "They always give it back when they're scared," she says. "Ask me again when they're not." Her fingers stop an inch from it.
failure.art: A translucent figure in goggles and blue coveralls pulling her gloved hand back from a blue ribbon held out by a teenager, young men in gowns frozen by an open trophy case

best.title: Opening Night
best.text: Dot asks for a hammer. At one in the morning, with Halloween barely over, the whole parlor holding boards and passing nails, she builds the drag night a real stage: pine planks, a proper apron, steps with hand-cut dovetails, and footlights wired off her father's drill, which is just a tool again, humming the way it was meant to. Trip comes down out of the endless hallway with sawdust in his hair, picks up the 1966 brass plate with his father's name on it, walks straight up to Dot and says the two words himself: "I'm sorry." Later, when Chad holds out a spare wig, Trip takes it and asks him, quietly, to teach him the walk. Lady Chadelier opens the show on Dot's stage, and Dot runs the light. At dawn she signs the underside of the stage, D.R. 1986, sets the drill on the cellar workbench, and walks down Old Quarry Road into the sunrise with her ribbon on, smiling, finished at last. Drag night raises enough to fix the Glitter Box roof twice over. That winter Gamma Rho takes down the trophy case and mails every trophy back to the women it belongs to, with a letter. The Gazette prints a correction. And next spring Glimmer Falls High hands out its first Dorothy Ruskin Blue Ribbon for joinery. The winner is a girl.
best.art: A lanky freckled translucent girl in blue coveralls and pink curlers wearing a blue ribbon on her chest, kneeling on a freshly built pine stage in a Victorian parlor with an old chrome drill in her hand, young men in sequined gowns and wigs holding up boards beside her, a gangly one in a towering blond wig posing under warm footlights, a young man in a letterman jacket holding a hammer, a tall drag queen in silver sequins applauding, pink dawn light through unboarded windows, wide shot

good.title: Lights Up
good.text: At dawn the screws back out of every door and window and fall to the floor like hail, and Gamma Rho staggers out into the sunshine in sequins and smeared lipstick. Trip is found on the porch swing, wrapped in a pink sleeping bag from 1958, shivering and very quiet. Drag night goes on the next weekend, and it is wonderful, and the Glitter Box gets a new roof. But the trophy case stays in the front hall, and the brothers learn to walk past it again. Every so often, a pledge dusting the glass finds a tiny, perfect drill hole in it that was not there the day before.
good.art: Exhausted young men in sequined gowns and smeared lipstick stumbling out of a Victorian house onto the porch into bright morning sunlight, loose screws scattered across the porch boards, a pale young man wrapped in a pink sleeping bag on the porch swing, a glowing glass trophy case visible through the open front door, warm morning light, wide shot

bittersweet.title: Righty Tighty
bittersweet.text: You get the brothers out through a cellar window at dawn, and Dot lets you go. But she keeps the house. Every door of the Gamma Rho house stays screwed shut from the outside, the college condemns it by Christmas, and drag night is cancelled, so the Glitter Box keeps its buckets one more winter. Trip comes back, but he never talks about the hallway. Out on Old Quarry Road the boarded house sits empty, and on its top porch step stands a coffee can of pink curlers that nobody in town will touch.
bittersweet.art: A boarded-up Victorian house at the end of a dark country road at dusk, every door and window crossed with planks fastened by rows of screws, a coffee can of pink foam curlers sitting alone on the top porch step, tall dark pines behind, a teenager standing at the gate, gray dusk light, wide shot

bad.title: The Long Hallway
bad.text: The hallway takes you, and it takes Trip, still clutching his camcorder. At the last second you shoved Chad toward the stairs, and he made it down. You are not hurt. You are just upstairs, in a hallway of identical doors that never ends, walking side by side with Trip in a flashlight beam, looking for the way down. Lady Chadelier opens every Glitter Box show after that with an empty chair saved in the front row. And the new pledges of Gamma Rho hear two voices upstairs, one calling "I'll be right back!" and the other begging him not to say it.
bad.art: An endless dim Victorian hallway of identical doors lit by a single flashlight beam, a teenager and a young man in a letterman jacket clutching a camcorder walking side by side away down it, faded floral wallpaper, and far behind them the faint glow of two round amber goggles, long one-point view down the hall
